text: ActRaiser is a 1990 video game developed by Quintet and published by Enix for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, combining traditional side-scrolling platforming with city-building elements. A sequel, ActRaiser 2, was released for the Super NES in 1993. In 2007, the game became available on the Wii's Virtual Console in Europe, North America, and Japan, and a mobile phone version was released in Europe in 2004 by Macrospace on September 1. A remake titled Actraiser Renaissance was released in September 2021 for Android, iOS, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Windows. The player controls "The Master," the main protagonist, though the Master is never directly controlled; instead, the player controls an angel during simulation sequences and an animated statue during action sequences. In the overhead simulation mode, the player protects and guides a new civilization starting with two humans, managing population growth through road planning and using miracles such as lightning, rain, sunlight, wind, and earthquakes. The angel can shoot monsters with arrows and guide the player on where to build and use miracles. Flying monsters originate from four lairs at the start of each level, spawning continuously until the population seals the lairs, which eventually eliminates all flying monsters and increases the civilization level, allowing advanced structures and higher population. The Master gains levels by increasing the world's population, which boosts hit points and SP for performing miracles. Each area features two side-scrolling action sequences—one before and one near the end—where the player controls the humanlike statue, jumping between platforms, defeating monsters, and earning a score, culminating in a boss fight. The final level is a boss marathon ending with a fight against Tanzra. The plot centers on "The Master" (known as God in the Japanese version) who was defeated by Tanzra (Satan in the Japanese version), also called "The Evil One," and retreated to a sky palace, where he fell into a deep sleep. Tanzra divided the world into six lands, each ruled by a lieutenant, who turned people to evil. After centuries, the Master awakens, finds his powers diminished due to lack of belief, and rebuilds civilizations by defeating Tanzra’s lieutenants and restoring faith through prayer. After defeating all lieutenants, he attacks Tanzra’s stronghold, Death Heim, and defeats him. Post-victory, the Master and his servant observe the civilizations and note that no one worships them anymore, as people now solve problems independently. They then return to the sky palace and depart into the heavens, awaiting future need. The game is an allegory for Judeo-Christian monotheism, with the protagonist named God and antagonist Satan in the original Japanese version. Due to Nintendo of America’s strict early 1990s policy against overt religious themes, the main character was renamed "The Master," though the allegorical elements remain, including the godly journey, miracles, and prayer. Bosses are based on real-world religion or mythology, such as Greek and Hindu traditions. The ending explores the loss of faith, as people no longer pray because they can solve problems on their own. For the North American release, the title was changed to ActRaiser with a new logo, monster lairs were replaced with skull-like symbols (from Stars of David), action segments were made easier with new enemy attacks, spells requiring less magic, spike pits not instantly killing the player, and more time per segment; simulation segments were made harder and it is difficult to reach the maximum experience level. A "Professional!" mode, unlocked after completing the game, contains only action segments with a level design similar to the original Japanese version. European releases use North American changes as a base, with the "Professional!" mode renamed to "Action" mode, available from the start, and both Story and Action modes offering three difficulties. Normal and Expert Story modes mirror the North American main and Japanese modes respectively, with a new Beginner mode easier than Normal. Normal Action mode resembles the North American Professional! mode, while Beginner Action mode mirrors the North American main mode but without the new enemy attacks. Expert Action mode is the most difficult, restoring new attacks, increasing enemy damage, and reducing player damage. A modified arcade version for the Nintendo Super System features only action stages, has a different scoring system, and is much harder than the retail version, with spike contact instantly fatal. A limited mobile version released in 2004 includes only the first three action levels, omitting town-building. The game's soundtrack, composed by Yuzo Koshiro, was released on a single disc in Japan on January 25, 1991, and a shorter arranged version, Symphonic Suite, on September 21. In 2004, a medley of the music was performed live at the second annual Symphonic Game Music Concert in Leipzig, Germany, and the soundtrack was re-released on vinyl and CD by Wayô Records in 2021 as ActRaiser Original Soundtrack & Symphonic Suite. Koshiro later fully recreated the original soundtrack for Actraiser Renaissance and composed fifteen new tracks in both original SNES sample quality and Renaissance’s higher audio quality. Micom BASIC Magazine ranked ActRaiser eighth in popularity in March 1991, and it received a 23.68/30 score in a 1993 Super Famicom Magazine readers' poll, placing 26th among Super Famicom titles. The game received generally favorable reviews, with a 79.25% rating based on eight reviews from GameRankings, and Super Gamer called it a brilliant mix of strategic gods gameplay and platforming. It was awarded Best Music of 1993 by Electronic Gaming Monthly and ranked 75th best console game of all time in 1997, praised for its unique gameplay and hypnotic atmosphere. Quintet reported sales of 620,000 copies worldwide: 400,000 in Japan, 180,000 in North America, and 40,000 in Europe. ActRaiser was inducted into GameSpot's Greatest Games of All Time in December 2003, ranked 150th best on a Nintendo System in Nintendo Power's Top 200 Games list, and ranked #1 on ScrewAttack's "Top 10 Big Names That Fell Off" list in 2007 (discussed positively) and #10 on their "Top 20 SNES Games" list. In 2018, Complex ranked it 33rd on their "The Best Super Nintendo Games of All Time" list, and in 2017, Gamesradar ranked it 23rd on its "The Best SNES Games of All Time" list, praising the gameplay as a good mix of 2D action and city-building. In 1995, Total! placed it 91st on its "Top 100 SNES Games" list.
